_: Name, description and badge live in src/resources/connectors.json so the console and the browser process cannot disagree about them.
rebrand: Coda is now branded Superhuman Docs. The product renamed; the API did not - the host is still coda.io, IDs still look like d-, fl-, ws-, org-, and the docs still say coda.io/apis. Do not confuse it with Superhuman Mail, which is a different product with a different connector. The API's own title is now "Superhuman Docs API" (1.6.0) and support is care@superhuman.com, but every host, path and ID prefix is unchanged.

personal_token.label: API token
personal_token.where: coda.io/account > API settings > Generate API token. Coda lets you restrict a token to a single doc; do that rather than issuing an unrestricted one.
notes: An unrestricted token inherits everything the person can see, which for most accounts is every doc they have ever been shared on.

GET /whoami reports `scoped` (true if the token is restricted) and `tokenName`. Check `scoped` on connect and warn if it is false - it is the only way to tell from the API side that the user handed over a key to their whole account.
There is no fixed prefix; the field is empty deliberately rather than forgotten.
No third-party OAuth flow exists for this REST API; tokens are the supported mechanism.
Tokens are unscoped by default and inherit the generating user's permissions - the restriction has to be applied when the token is made.
Some autogenerated Swagger clients do not handle bearer auth correctly. Coda says so themselves; use a plain HTTP client.

ids.note: Every resource carries id, type and href. Most endpoints accept a name in place of an ID, and Coda's own documentation discourages it in almost every parameter description: names are changed by doc users, and where several objects share a name an ARBITRARY one is selected - silently, with no error. Always resolve to an ID and store that.
ids.prefixes: doc ids are bare (AbCDeFGH); pages canvas-, tables grid-, columns c-, rows i-, controls ctrl-, formulas f-, folders fl-, workspaces ws-, organizations org-.

pagination.rule: The maximum page size can change at any time and differs per endpoint. Asking for more than the maximum silently returns the maximum, so page on the presence of nextPageToken - never on the result count matching the limit requested.
pagination.page_token: A pageToken implies every parameter from the original request. Any other parameter sent alongside one is ignored.

consistency.note: The single most important behaviour of this API, and the one that makes naive write-then-read code wrong.
consistency.writes_are_async: Every mutating endpoint returns HTTP 202, not 200. The edit is accepted and queued, usually applied within a few seconds, and it can still FAIL after the 202 if invalid. A 202 is not success.
consistency.mutation_status: Each such response carries a requestId. GET /mutationStatus/{requestId} reports { completed, warning }. Poll it rather than assuming. Status is not kept for more than about a day.
consistency.reads_are_snapshots: Doc data (rows, pages, columns) comes from the most recent snapshot and can lag what the browser shows. Sending the header X-Coda-Doc-Version: latest makes the API return HTTP 400 instead of stale data - use it when correctness matters more than availability.
consistency.realtime_lag: Edits made in the Coda UI also take a few seconds to become visible to the API.
consistency.volatile_formulas: Today(), Now() and User() behave differently through the API. Time values may only be current to the doc's last edit, and user values may be blank or invalid. Do not read a User() column and expect the caller's identity.

whoami.notes: The connect-time check. Returns name, loginId, workspace, and crucially `scoped` and `tokenName`.

list_docs.notes: Only docs the user has opened at least once, ordered by the latest event relevant to them. A doc shared but never opened does not appear. Rate limited far harder than other reads - 4 requests per 6 seconds.

get_doc.notes: docSize.overApiSizeLimit is worth checking before a big read.

get_page.notes: contentType is canvas, embed or syncPage. isEffectivelyHidden accounts for a hidden parent, isHidden does not.

list_page_content.notes: Plain text only. For html or markdown use the export flow below.

export_page.notes: Asynchronous: returns an export id, then poll GET .../export/{requestId} until status completes and read downloadLink. The link expires quickly and a fresh one is issued on each status call, so fetch immediately or re-poll. This is a read despite being a POST.

params.visibleOnly: boolean? - base tables only, ignored on views

list_columns.notes: Call this before reading rows. Column IDs are immutable; names are not, and row values are keyed by column ID unless useColumnNames is set.

list_rows.notes: syncToken is the incremental-sync mechanism: the response carries nextSyncToken, and passing it back later returns only what has since changed. Use it instead of re-reading a whole table on a schedule.

params.keyColumns: string[]? - column IDs to match on

upsert_rows.notes: Base tables only - not views. Without keyColumns it inserts and returns addedRowIds; with them it upserts and addedRowIds is absent. If several rows match the key, ALL of them are updated. Always 202.

update_row.notes: Addressing by name updates an arbitrary matching row. Use the row ID.

get_formula.notes: Returns the computed value. A cheap way to read a rollup without pulling the table it summarises.

resolve_browser_link.notes: Turns a coda.io URL the user pasted into an API href. The natural first call when a task starts from a link rather than an ID.

value_formats.simple: Default. Strings, numbers and booleans; arrays such as multiselects are flattened to comma-delimited strings - which is lossy and will split a value that itself contains a comma.
value_formats.simpleWithArrays: As simple, but arrays stay arrays. Prefer this over simple for anything programmatic.
value_formats.rich: Lossless. Text comes back as Markdown (plain text is fenced with triple backticks), and currency, lookup, image, person and hyperlink values come back as JSON-LD objects with @context and @type - MonetaryAmount, StructuredValue, ImageObject, Person, WebPage. Use this when the value has to survive a round trip.

never_expose: POST /docs/{docId}/tables/{t}/rows/{r}/buttons/{c} - pushing a button. Coda's own note: the token only needs write access to that table, but the button can perform ANY action on the document, including writing to other tables and invoking Pack actions against third-party services. It is an arbitrary-code trigger wearing a write permission, and nothing in the Flux catalogue justifies it.
POST /docs/{docId}/hooks/automation/{ruleId} - triggering an automation. Same objection: the payload runs whatever the rule does.
DELETE on docs, pages, rows and folders, and DELETE .../pages/{p}/content with no elementIds, which erases the whole page.
The acl endpoints - adding a permission shares a document with someone, and suppressEmail does it without telling them.
POST /docs/{docId}/publish - publishes to the public web, with a discoverable flag.
gotchas: sortBy=natural implies visibleOnly=true. Sending sortBy=natural with visibleOnly=false explicitly is a 400, not a silently-ignored parameter.

Creating a doc or page, and renaming a doc or page, requires the token owner to be a Doc Maker or Admin in the workspace. Editors can be auto-promoted if the workspace allows it, which means an innocuous createDoc call can change the user's role.
Insert and upsert work on base tables only. Pointing them at a view fails.
Page analytics returns 401 - not 403 - if the doc is not in an Enterprise workspace. Do not treat that 401 as a bad token.
Coda reserves the right to remove APIs with three months' notice, announced in their community rather than in the reference.

rate_limits.note: Per user, shared across every endpoint in the same class and across all docs - not per token and not per doc. Coda says these are subject to change without notice, so a 429 is the authority and every script must back off and retry.

also_ships.mcp: Coda publishes an MCP server they describe as optimised for LLM usage patterns and often exposing more granular methods than this REST API. Worth revisiting if a skill outgrows the endpoints above.
also_ships.spec: OpenAPI 3.0 spec in YAML and JSON, importable straight into Postman.

admin_api.note: A separate surface from the doc API above, for organisation administration rather than reading content. Flux does not use it and should not: it is enterprise-only, admin-only, and every useful call needs an organizationId the personal token above cannot produce. Recorded so nobody re-derives it or mistakes it for the doc API.
admin_api.auth: Same bearer token header. Access is limited to enterprise organisations, and only organisation admins can call it for their own org.

shape.hierarchy: organization > workspace > folder > doc > page. Most paths are nested under /organizations/{organizationId}, and the newer doc routes additionally nest under /workspaces/{workspaceId} - the un-nested equivalents still exist but are marked deprecated.
shape.pagination: items, nextPageToken and nextPageLink. limit is 1-500 and defaults to 100, but the maximum can change and can differ per endpoint - page on the presence of nextPageToken, never on the result count matching the limit requested.
shape.page_token: A pageToken implies every parameter from the original request. Any other parameter sent alongside one is ignored.

reads_worth_knowing.audit_events: GET /organizations/{org}/audit/events - login/logout and essentially every mutation, filterable by action, entityType, entityId, user, container and time. The entity types now include agentInstance and agentToolCall, so AI agent activity is audited alongside everything else.
reads_worth_knowing.docs: GET /organizations/{org}/docs - searchable, with sharing filters (sharedWithAnyone, sharedWithExternalDomain, sharedWithDomains) that are the fastest way to find over-shared docs.
reads_worth_knowing.page_content: GET .../pages/{pageId}?outputFormat=LossyPlainText - the only way this API returns actual page text. Anything richer goes through the export flow.
reads_worth_knowing.export: POST .../export then poll GET .../export/{exportId}. PDF, Plaintext or HTML. Download links last about 5 minutes and a fresh one is issued on each status call, so fetch immediately or re-poll.

webhooks.handshake: On create, and again whenever the target URL changes, Coda GETs the target with an X-Webhook-Code header. The target must answer 200 or 204 and echo that header back. POST .../webhooks/{id}/reset re-runs it.
webhooks.signature: X-Webhook-Signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the stringified POST body, keyed with the signatureKey on the webhook object. Note the differences from most vendors: hex not base64, the body alone with no id or timestamp prefix, and therefore no replay protection from the signature at all.
webhooks.delivery: 10-second timeout, exponential backoff, disabled after 8 hours of consecutive failures. Deliveries can repeat, and once delivered they cannot be replayed - so a receiver must deduplicate and a gap must be backfilled through the events endpoint.

never_expose: Everything under /legalHolds - creating a hold changes what an organisation is legally obliged to retain.
The permission endpoints on docs and folders. bypassOrgExternalSharingRestrictions on the add-permission call does exactly what it says.
Organization user activate/deactivate, and its bypassScim flag, which deliberately desynchronises Coda from the customer's identity provider.
Transfer user resources, delete doc, delete folder, and the workspace role endpoints.

source.note: Taken verbatim from the Superhuman Docs Admin API reference (version 0.0.2) the user supplied. Coda publishes an OpenAPI 3.0 spec for it, which is the thing to fetch if this is ever actually implemented.

notes: Rewritten from the Superhuman Docs API reference (1.6.0) itself. Every path, parameter, rate limit and behaviour above is taken verbatim from it.

This CORRECTS the previous revision, which was search-verified and said the limit was 10 requests per second per token. It is neither per-second nor per-token: five separate per-user classes, the tightest being 4 requests per 6 seconds for listing docs.
The previous revision also missed that every write returns 202 and can fail afterwards. Code written against it would have treated a queued edit as a completed one.
The admin_api block below is a different surface with its own source and was already vendor-docs.
